pull_quote: It’s best to read just one or two of Ahern’s fables at a time so you can truly appreciate their wit, pathos and imagination

title: Juliet the Maniac
author: Juliet Escoria
pull_quote: Dubbed ‘The Bell Jar’ for the modern age, this autobiographical novel about a teenager’s road to recovery from bioplar disorder and drugs, cements Escoria’s status as one of the most powerful voices in independent literature

title: Frankissstein
author: Jeanette Winterson review
pull_quote: Jeanette Winterson’s re-imagining of ‘Frankenstein’ includes a world of smart-tech and artificial intelligence – even cryogenic freezing and sex robots

title: The Ottoman Secret
author: Raymond Khoury review
pull_quote: This alternative history in which Europe is ruled by an autocratic sultan will appeal to fans of ‘The Handmaid’s Tale’

title: City of Girls
author: Elizabeth Gilbert
pull_quote: The new novel from the author of 'Eat, Pray, Love' is a tale of love and loss in New York City, which shows she is as gifted a novelist, as she is a memoirist

title: Big Sky
author: Kate Atkinson review
pull_quote: After a nine-year hiatus, Atkinson returns to the gruff-but-loveable private detective Jackson Brodie, who in the intervening years has been played onscreen by Jason Isaacs in ‘Case Histories’

title: Game Changer
author: Shahid Afridi with Wajahat S Khan review
pull_quote: Sometimes spiky, undoubtedly opinionated, former Pakistan cricket captain is a warrior both on and off the field

title: Night Boat to Tangier
author: Kevin Barry
pull_quote: As two Irish gangsters sit in the port of Algeciras waiting for a 23-year old named Dilly, their vaudevillian patter reminds you of Didi and Gogo in Beckett’s ‘Waiting for Godot’

title: Live a Little
author: Howard Jacobson
pull_quote: The Man Booker Prize-winning author of ‘The Finkler Question’ writes impressively about ninety-plus-year-olds, while indulging in wordplay and biting political commentary

title: The Most Fun We Ever Had
author: Claire Lombardo
pull_quote: A complex and believable family saga that unfolds with the sudden appearance of a teenage boy given up for adoption years ago

title: Sweet Sorrow
author: David Nicholls
pull_quote: Bag a copy immediately, because this has got ‘perfect summer read’ smeared all over it like so much factor 30

title: I Am Sovereign
author: Nicola Barker
pull_quote: This restlessly inventive, postmodern take on fictional narrative has echoes of Virginia Woolf’s attempts to capture individual consciousness

title: Lady in the Lake
author: Laura Lippman
pull_quote: This vivid historical crime novel follows Maddie whose post-divorce life finds her trying to solve a murder

title: The Perfect Wife
author: JP Delaney
pull_quote: This new psychological thriller about a Silicon Valley tycoon and his made-to-order, robotic wife is the kind of novel words like ‘unputdownable’ were invented for

title: Is There Still Sex in the City?
author: Candace Bushnell
pull_quote: The wit that made this former girl-about-town’s columns so appealing is gone, replaced by poisonous tropes about single women and bizarre attempts to coin new slang

title: Trick Mirror
author: Jia Tolentino
pull_quote: Jia Tolentino’s collection of essays speaks like no other to the millennial condition, writes Adam White

title: Quichotte
author: Salman Rushdie review
pull_quote: It’s a fast-spinning postmodern double Catherine wheel – impossible not to be dazzled by, but also making a lot of choking smoke

title: Akin
author: Emma Donoghue
pull_quote: The Irish-Canadian author’s first contemporary novel for adults since ‘Room’, which was a finalist for the Booker Prize in 2010, is a profoundly human portrayal of a life disrupted by the opioid crisis

title: Year of the Monkey
author: Patti Smith
pull_quote: In her new memoir, the singer-songwriter, poet and author is haunted by insidious insomnia, the martial ticking of the clock and the spectre of climate change

title: Girl
author: Edna O'Brien
pull_quote: An astonishing act of imaginative empathy on O’Brien’s part, grounded in research trips to Nigeria, and interviews with people involved on the ground

title: How to Make the World Add Up
author: Tim Harford
pull_quote: Characteristic lucidity, concealed intellectual depths, wry humour - and a big unifying idea - from one of our finest economic and statistical communicators

title: Beautiful World, Where Are You
author: Sally Rooney review
pull_quote: The Irish novelist is now a major literary ‘somebody’ and writes sharply and discerningly about her fellow millennials. But with one exception, it is hard to care about her characters

title: Her Heart for a Compass
author: Sarah Ferguson review
pull_quote: Duchess of York’s novel is chaste by Mills & Boon standards, but manages to go against convention in other more pleasing ways

title: Spare
author: Prince Harry review
pull_quote: His wife might be the natural on camera, but the Duke of Sussex hits his stride on paper in this breathtakingly frank book

title: Victory City
author: Salman Rushdie review
pull_quote: In his first novel since last summer’s brutal on-stage attack, Salman Rushdie’s exuberant writing remains a source of pleasure

title: Books of the month: From Colson Whitehead’s Crook Manifesto to Unseen
author: Selina Mills
pull_quote: Martin Chilton reviews the biggest new books for July in our monthly column

title: The House of Beckham
author: Tom Bower review
pull_quote: The biographer behind books about everyone from Boris Johnson to Meghan and Harry has turned his gaze to the Beckhams, but this Wikipedia-esque tome retreads old rumours and will fail to shock many

title: A Voyage Around the Queen
author: Craig Brown
pull_quote: Craig Brown applies his kaleidoscopic approach to biography in a fascinating exploration of the Queen’s life and our attitudes to monarchy, writes Katie Rosseinsky

title: The Golden Road
author: William Dalrymple
pull_quote: Forget the Silk Roads, it’s the Golden Road we should be celebrating. Renowned historian William Dalrymple argues that, thanks to its major role in global trade between AD300 and 600, it’s India, rather than China, to which we owe some of the most important developments in human civilisation, writes

title: I Want You to Be Happy
author: Jem Calder
pull_quote: Abandon your Monzo pots, ye who enter here! Jem Calder’s debut novel, about a millennial copywriter and a wannabe Gen Z poet, captures modern life at its most expensive, overwhelming and bleak – but the book is ultimately hopeful, he tells Jessie Thompson

title: Cold Sunset
author: William Boyd
pull_quote: Endless cigarettes, copious drink, and a succession of glamorous hotel rooms and restaurants set the scene for Boyd’s intoxicating world
